name: Normandy landings
info: On 6 June 1944 American, British and Canadian forces, with airborne troops and a fleet drawn from eight navies, landed on five beaches on the Normandy coast, opening the liberation of France and Western Europe.

facts.date: 6 June 1944 (D-Day), after a postponement of 24 hours from the 5 June first chosen
facts.place: An 80-kilometre stretch of the Normandy coast of France, divided into the sectors Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, with airborne landings inland
facts.sides: The Allies under General Dwight D. Eisenhower, with General Bernard Montgomery commanding the land forces, nearly 160,000 troops crossing the Channel on the day; Germany under Hitler, with Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt as Supreme Commander West and Field Marshal Erwin Rommel commanding Army Group B
facts.outcome: The Allies established a beachhead at each of the five sites on the first day, but Carentan, Saint-Lô, Bayeux and Caen stayed in German hands; the five beachheads were not connected until 12 June.

t: The landings were the largest seaborne invasion in history: a fleet of 6,939 vessels from eight navies, nearly 160,000 troops across the Channel on D-Day and 875,000 landed by the end of June.
Allied casualties on the first day were at least 10,000, with 4,414 confirmed dead; German casualties are estimated at 4,000 to 9,000. Omaha, with its high cliffs, had the most Allied casualties.

Many of the first-day objectives were not met: Caen, a major objective, was not completely captured until 21 July, and the Germans never achieved Hitler's stated aim of throwing the Allies back into the sea.
dyk: The day was chosen because the tides, the hour and the moon allowed only a few dates a month; when storms forced a postponement from 5 June, the next suitable dates were two weeks later, and a major storm struck the Normandy coast from 19 to 22 June.
ev: The decision to undertake a cross-channel invasion within the next year is taken at the Trident Conference in Washington in May
Eisenhower and Montgomery first see the plan and insist on widening the landings to five divisions
On 4 June Eisenhower meets Group Captain James Stagg, whose forecast of improving weather leads him to go ahead on 6 June
On 6 June airborne troops land after midnight and the amphibious landings on the five beaches begin about 06:30
On 12 June the five beachheads are connected
German forces retreat east across the Seine, closing Operation Overlord

sections.background:
After the German Army invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin pressed his new allies to create a second front in western Europe. In May 1942 the Soviet Union and the United States announced a full understanding on the urgent tasks of creating one that year, but Winston Churchill persuaded Franklin D. Roosevelt to postpone it, since even with American help the Allies lacked adequate forces. The western Allies instead fought in the Mediterranean, winning in North Africa by mid-1943 and invading Sicily in July and the Italian mainland in September.

The decision to cross the Channel within the next year was taken at the Trident Conference in May 1943, and at Tehran in November 1943 Roosevelt and Churchill promised Stalin a second front in May 1944. Planning was limited by the number of landing craft, most of which were committed in the Mediterranean and Pacific. Four sites were considered: Brittany, the Cotentin Peninsula, Normandy and the Pas-de-Calais. The first two were peninsulas, which the Germans could cut off at a narrow isthmus. The Pas-de-Calais, the closest point to Britain, was the most heavily fortified and offered few chances to expand. Normandy would allow threats to Cherbourg, to the ports of Brittany and to Paris, and its lack of ports was to be met by artificial Mulberry harbours.

Eisenhower and Montgomery thought the first plan, three divisions on a 40-kilometre front, too small and insisted on five divisions and three airborne ones. The extra landing craft this needed delayed the invasion from May to June.
sections.forces:
The Allied command was General Dwight D. Eisenhower at the head of the Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force, with General Bernard Montgomery commanding the 21st Army Group. The First Army, under Lieutenant General Omar Bradley, landed about 73,000 men, 15,600 of them airborne, at Utah and Omaha. The Second Army, under Lieutenant General Sir Miles Dempsey, put ashore 83,115 men, 61,715 of them British, at Gold, Juno and Sword. The fleet, under Admiral Sir Bertram Ramsay, numbered 6,939 vessels from eight navies, including 1,213 warships and 4,126 landing craft, with 195,700 naval personnel. Specialised tanks nicknamed Hobart's Funnies, and Duplex-Drive amphibious tanks, supported the landings.

Germany had fifty divisions in France and the Low Countries. Combat losses, above all on the Eastern Front, meant its soldiers were on average six years older than the Allies', and many in Normandy were Ostlegionen with captured equipment and little motor transport. Seven of the eleven panzer or panzergrenadier divisions in France were not fully operational or only partly mobile in early June. Rommel ordered stakes, tripods, mines and obstacles on the beaches and tripled the mines along the coast, though he reported construction in some areas only 18 per cent complete.

The German commanders disagreed over the armoured reserves: Rommel wanted tanks close to the coast, Rundstedt and Geyr wanted them concentrated further back. Hitler left three Panzer divisions under Geyr, gave Rommel control of three, and kept four himself.
sections.course:
The Allies deceived the Germans about the date and place of the landing through Operation Bodyguard, including a fictitious army group under Patton, and on the eve of the invasion dummy paratroopers and strips of metal foil were used to suggest further landings. The first Allied action was the glider capture of the Caen canal and Orne river bridges, afterwards Pegasus Bridge, at 00:16. American airborne landings began with pathfinders at 00:15, but cloud scattered the paratroopers; after 24 hours only about a third of those dropped were under their divisions' control. Sainte-Mère-Église was the first town liberated.

Bombing began about midnight, but was largely ineffective at Omaha, where low cloud and fear of hitting the troops led many bombers to release late. The naval bombardment of the beaches began at 05:50. At Utah the 8th Infantry Regiment landed at 06:30, about 1,800 metres from the intended place, and the 4th Infantry Division landed 21,000 troops for 197 casualties. Omaha was the most heavily defended beach, held by the 352nd Infantry Division rather than the single regiment expected. Currents and fire cost the landing force dearly, 27 of 32 amphibious tanks sank, and by late morning barely 600 men had reached the higher ground.

At Gold, Juno and Sword the landings began from 07:25. Towns were cleared in house-to-house fighting, specialised tanks disabled the strongpoints at Le Hamel and elsewhere, and at 16:00 the 21st Panzer Division counter-attacked between Sword and Juno before meeting stiff resistance.
sections.aftermath:
Nearly 160,000 troops crossed the Channel on D-Day, and 875,000 men had landed by the end of June. Allied casualties on the first day were at least 10,000, with 4,414 confirmed dead, and the Germans had 4,000 to 9,000 casualties, whether killed, wounded, missing or captured. Civilian casualties on D-Day and the day after are estimated at 3,000. The Germans had ordered French civilians not essential to the war effort to leave potential combat zones in Normandy.

The build-up of troops and the secure bridgehead came with fewer casualties than expected, but the plan had called for the capture of Carentan, Saint-Lô, Caen and Bayeux on the first day, with the beaches other than Utah linked, and none of these objectives was achieved. At Omaha the objectives were reached by 9 June. The five beachheads were connected on 12 June, when the Allies held a front about 97 kilometres long and 24 kilometres deep. Caen was not completely captured until 21 July, and German forces retreated east across the Seine on 30 August 1944, closing Operation Overlord.

The Allied victory is put down to several factors: the German defences were only partly finished, the deceptions left the Germans to defend a huge coastline, and Rommel and other commanders and troops were absent because of the forecast storms. The Allies held air supremacy, bombers and the French Resistance disrupted transport, specialised armour worked well except at Omaha, and German command was indecisive and overcomplicated.
sections.sources:
The history of the landings rests on the records of both sides and on later testimony. The record of the airborne preparations includes the BBC war correspondent Robert Barr's description of the paratroopers boarding their aircraft, and the German side is represented by the memoir of the armaments minister Albert Speer, published in 1969, which recalls the German high command's fear of airborne attacks on Hamburg and Bremen.

The figures for the dead and wounded are ranges and estimates. German casualties are put at 4,000 to 9,000, and Allied casualties on the first day at least 10,000, of whom 4,414 are confirmed dead. Casualties for individual beaches are estimates too, for instance about 1,000 at Gold, 961 at Juno and as high as 1,000 at Sword, and the 3,000 civilian casualties are also an estimate. A 1965 report by the Counter-insurgency Information Analysis Center gives the results of the French Resistance's sabotage, saying that 52 locomotives were destroyed in the south-east on 6 June and that Normandy was isolated as of 7 June.

The naval planning is judged by later writers: the historian Correlli Barnett called it a never surpassed masterpiece of planning. The reasons for the Allied success listed by historians include German weakness, the deceptions, air supremacy and the weather.
sections.legacy:
The Normandy landings began the liberation of France and the rest of Western Europe and laid the foundations for the Allied victory on the Western Front. The Allies, who had promised Stalin a second front at Tehran, now had one, and the Germans never achieved Hitler's stated aim of throwing them back into the sea, either on D-Day or at any time afterwards.

Memorials and museums mark the coast. At Omaha Beach parts of the Mulberry harbour are still visible, and the Normandy American Cemetery and Memorial lies nearby at Colleville-sur-Mer. Pointe du Hoc is little changed from 1944, with its bomb craters and most of its concrete bunkers. At Pegasus Bridge the bridge was replaced in 1994 by one of similar appearance, and the original stands in the grounds of a nearby museum. Sections of Mulberry Harbour B remain in the sea at Arromanches, and the Longues-sur-Mer battery is well preserved. The Juno Beach Centre opened in 2003, funded by the Canadian federal and provincial governments, France and Canadian veterans. The British Normandy Memorial above Gold Beach, designed by Liam O'Connor, opened in 2021, and two German military cemeteries are nearby.

In July 2026 UNESCO designated the Beaches of the D-Day Landings a World Heritage Site.

summary: On 6 June 1944 Allied troops landed from the sea and the air on five beaches in Normandy, the largest seaborne invasion in history. They secured a foothold on the first day but not their main objectives, and the German retreat across the Seine on 30 August closed Operation Overlord.
references: Antony Beevor, D-Day: The Battle for Normandy (Viking, 2009)
Max Hastings, Overlord: D-Day and the Battle for Normandy (Joseph, 1984)
L.F. Ellis, Victory in the West, Volume I: The Battle of Normandy (Naval & Military Press, 2004)
Peter Caddick-Adams, Sand and Steel: A New History of D-Day (Hutchinson, 2019)
Stephen Ambrose, D-Day June 6, 1944: The Climactic Battle of World War II (Simon & Schuster, 1994)
Ken Ford, Overlord: The D-Day Landings (Osprey, 2009)
notes: The article's lead names Operation Neptune; the landings are the first phase of Operation Overlord. I kept both names in the text only where needed.

Casualty figures: Allied at least 10,000 with 4,414 confirmed dead; German 4,000-9,000; civilian about 3,000 for D-Day and D+1. Beach-by-beach figures (Utah 197, Omaha around 2,000, Gold 1,000, Juno 961, Sword as high as 1,000) are the article's and not additive; I gave only some in the text.

The article has no section on sources or historiography. My 'sources' section is built from what it does say: Barr, Speer, the 1965 report, Barnett and the ranges on losses. It is thin and the editor may wish to replace or trim it.
Omaha: the article says casualties 'around 2,000' in the narrative; I did not put that into the course section.

Left out: the Pointe du Hoc action in detail, Pegasus Bridge detail, Merville Battery, the French Resistance plans (Vert, Bleu, Tortue, Violet), the Maharbal-style anecdotes (none), Speer's quotation, Lovat's piper, the Victoria Cross, details of airborne losses on the Dives, naval losses (Svenner, Corry) and the executions of French collaborators at Pointe du Hoc.
The article says Allied naval force had five battleships, 20 cruisers, 65 destroyers, two monitors; not used.
Inconsistency in the article: 'nearly 5,000 landing and assault craft' in the aftermath against 4,126 landing craft in the naval section; I used 4,126 only.

The article says Utah was not among the beaches to be linked ('all the beaches (other than Utah) linked'), yet the lead says only Juno and Gold were linked on the first day and all five not until 12 June; I followed the lead and the aftermath for the 12 June date.
The article's own 'D-Day' phrase and 'largest seaborne invasion in history' are given as its statements.
UNESCO designation in July 2026 is stated in the article's last line.
